brief: n monsters stand in a circle; monster i has a_i health and when killed explodes for b_i damage to the next monster (monster n wraps to 1). Each bullet does 1 damage; find the minimum bullets to kill all monsters.
key_idea: Pick the start monster to shoot; every other monster i gets free damage b_{i-1} from its predecessor, so bullets on i are max(0, a_i - b_{i-1}); the start monster must be shot a_i times instead, so add the cheapest penalty min(a_i, b_{i-1}).
solution: Let c_i = max(0, a_i - b_{i-1}) (indices mod n); c_i is the bullets needed for i if its predecessor explodes first.
Let S = sum of c_i over all i; the circle is broken at one point where the chain must start.
Chain-start choice: the monster j that is not helped by its predecessor costs a_j instead of c_j, extra cost a_j - c_j = min(a_j, b_{j-1}).
Answer = S + min over j of (a_j - c_j). Since the chain is a cycle, one break point suffices.
Edge cases: a_i and b_i up to 1e12, so use 64-bit integers; n >= 2.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: Answer = S + min = 4 + 2 = 6, which matches the sample output.

brief: Keshi invites a subset of n friends; friend i has i dollars and is happy only if at most a_i invited friends are richer and at most b_i invited friends are poorer. Find the maximum number of friends that can be invited with everyone happy.
key_idea: Feasibility is monotone in k (removing the poorest invitee keeps everyone happy), so binary search k; for fixed k, scan friends richest to poorest and invite i when cnt <= a_i and k-1-cnt <= b_i.
solution: Binary search the answer k in [0, n]; k = 0 is always feasible.
For a fixed k, the j-th invited friend in decreasing wealth has exactly j richer invited friends, so friend i can sit at position cnt iff k-1-b_i <= cnt <= a_i.
Scan i = n down to 1 with cnt = 0; invite i whenever cnt < k and it fits position cnt, then cnt++.
Greedy is optimal by exchange: if an optimal solution fills position cnt with a later-scanned friend, swapping in i (which also fits) keeps it valid.
k is feasible iff the scan reaches cnt = k; the answer is the largest feasible k.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: k=3: i=3 needs 0 in [1,1] no; i=2 needs 0 in [1,2] no... cnt stays 0 until i=1 takes it (0 in [0,1]); cnt=1 != 3, infeasible.
k=2: i=3 needs cnt=0 in [0,1], take, cnt=1; i=2 needs cnt=1 in [0,2], take, cnt=2 == k, feasible.
Binary search gives answer 2, matching the sample output.

brief: Given an array of n integers, output exactly three range operations; each operation adds to a segment [l,r] values that are multiples of the segment length, so that all elements become zero.
key_idea: Zero a_1 with a length-1 operation, multiply every other a_i by n using the length-(n-1) operation on [2,n], then cancel everything with the length-n operation on [1,n].
solution: If n = 1, print three operations on [1,1]: add -a_1, then 0, then 0.
Operation 1: [1,1], add -a_1, so position 1 becomes 0.
Operation 2: [2,n] (length n-1), add (n-1)*a_i to each i >= 2, so a_i becomes n*a_i.
Operation 3: [1,n] (length n), add 0 to position 1 and -n*a_i to each i >= 2; each value is divisible by n, so all elements become 0.
Magnitudes stay within 64-bit (|a_i * n| <= 1e14). Many outputs are valid, so check by simulation rather than matching the sample text.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space (output size)
dry_run: Op2 [2,4] length 3 add 9, 6, 12: [0, 12, 8, 16] (each equals 4*a_i).
Op3 [1,4] length 4 add 0, -12, -8, -16 (all divisible by 4): [0, 0, 0, 0].

brief: n kangaroos with integer sizes; a kangaroo of size x can hold one of size y only if x >= 2y, and a held kangaroo cannot hold another. Minimize the number of visible (unheld) kangaroos.
key_idea: Sort sizes; the optimal matching of m pairs uses the m smallest as held and the m largest as holders, so greedily match the small half with the smallest available big kangaroo at least twice its size.
solution: Sort the sizes ascending.
Small candidates are indices 0..n/2-1; holder candidates are indices from n/2 upward.
For each small i in increasing order, advance pointer j to the first index with s[j] >= 2*s[i]; if it exists, count a pair and move j forward.
Stop when j runs past the end.
Answer = n - (number of pairs).
complexity: O(n log n) time (sorting), O(n) space
dry_run: i=3 (5): need >= 10, j=7 (9) fails, j moves to 8, stop.
pairs = 3, answer = 8 - 3 = 5, matching the sample.

brief: Given an array a and an integer k, each step either decreases one element by 1 or copies one element's value into another element. Find the minimum number of steps so that the array sum is at most k.
key_idea: Unverified: the natural model (copy the minimum into the t largest, then decrement) matches samples 1-3 but gives 16 on sample 4 where the fetched sample output says 7, so the fetched sample text may be wrong.
solution: Sort descending and let S be the total sum; if S <= k the answer is 0.
Candidate plan: copy the minimum value m into the t largest elements (cost 1 each, saving a_i - m each), then decrement the remaining excess.
Cost of the plan = t + max(0, S - sum of savings - k); take the minimum over t from 0 to n-1.
Caveat: this plan does not reproduce fetched sample 4 (expects 7). A hand lower-bound check gives 9 for that input, so the statement or sample text should be re-checked before relying on this.
Possibility not analyzed: decreasing the minimum to 0 or below first as a copy source may cut cost further.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Minimum is 2, matching the sample.
Sample 4 under this model: minimum cost 16, versus expected 7 in the fetched text.

brief: Doremy has n contests, contest i is available on day i with difficulty a_i, and starts with IQ q. On day i she may test contest i only while IQ > 0; testing a contest with a_i > IQ lowers IQ by 1. Output a binary string maximizing the number of tested contests.
key_idea: Not reliably solved: the simple rule 'test every day while IQ > 0' gives 3 on sample 5 where the expected count is 4, so it is wrong; the correct exchange rule was not established.
solution: Facts: IQ never increases; a contest with a_i <= IQ costs nothing; a contest with a_i > IQ costs 1 IQ point.
Rejected rule: test every contest while IQ > 0. On sample 5 (q=2, a = 5 1 2 4 3) it tests days 1, 2, 3 and stops at 3, but skipping day 1 keeps IQ at 2 and tests 4 contests.
So the decision on expensive early contests depends on later ones, and a correct method needs an exchange or DP argument that was not verified here.
Do not use this record for solving; re-derive from the official editorial.
complexity: unknown (not established)
dry_run: Sample 4: n=4, q=2, a = 1 4 3 1. Testing days 1, 2, 3 (IQ 2, then 1, then 0) gives 3 tests, output 1110, matching the sample.
Sample 5: n=5, q=2, a = 5 1 2 4 3. Skipping day 1 and testing days 2..5 gives IQ 2, 2, 1, 0 with 4 tests, output 01111, matching the sample.
Naive rule on sample 5 tests only 3 contests, so it is wrong.

brief: Given a string s of n lowercase letters and k, split all letters into k non-empty strings (letters can be rearranged inside each). Minimize the lexicographically largest of these k strings and print that value.
key_idea: Sort the letters. If the first and k-th smallest differ, the answer is s[k-1] alone; otherwise the answer is the shared letter followed by the leftovers, which collapse to one repeated letter when they are all equal.
solution: Sort s ascending.
If s[0] != s[k-1]: print s[k-1]. Every one of the k strings must start with a letter at most s[k-1], and the largest string cannot be smaller than that letter.
Else the first k letters all equal c = s[0]; each of the k strings starts with c, and the answer begins with c.
Let rest = s[k..n-1] (sorted). If rest is a single repeated letter d, append d repeated ceil(|rest|/k) times, spreading it over k strings.
Otherwise append all of rest in sorted order (the one string that gets the leftovers is then the largest).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space per test
dry_run: Sample 1: s = baba, k = 2, sorted aabb: s[0] = s[1] = a, rest = bb (all b), ceil(2/2) = 1, answer ab.
Sample 2: s = baacb, k = 2, sorted aabbc: s[0] = s[1] = a, rest = bbc (not uniform), answer a + bbc = abbc.
Sample 3: s = baacb, k = 3, sorted aabbc: s[0] = a != s[2] = b, answer b.
Sample 6: s = phoenix, k = 1, sorted ehinopx: s[0] = s[0], rest = hinopx, answer ehinopx (whole sorted string).

brief: Start from an n x n zero matrix. Type 1 sets a whole row to a permutation of 1..n; type 2 sets a whole column to a permutation. Maximize the final sum using at most 2n operations and print the sum with the operations.
key_idea: Only the last operation touching each cell matters; order ops R1, C1, R2, C2, ... so each op owns a set of cells (R_k owns k-1 cells, C_k owns k cells) and gives its owned cells the largest available values.
solution: Each final cell value comes from the last operation covering its row or column. In the order R1, C1, R2, C2, ..., Rn, Cn: R_k owns cells (k, j) for j < k; C_k owns cells (i, k) for i <= k. Ownership counts are 0,1,1,2,2,...,n-1,n-1,n, which sum to n^2.
An operation owning m cells can place the top m values n, n-1, ..., n-m+1 on exactly those cells; the other cells of that line get the remaining values in any order.
Maximum sum = sum over k of T(k-1) + T(k), where T(m) = m*n - m(m-1)/2 is the sum of the m largest values. For n=2 this gives 7, matching the sample.
Output the total, then 2n lines: type, index, and the permutation built as above.
Confidence is medium: the construction matches the n=1 and n=2 samples, but optimality for larger n was argued, not brute-force checked.
complexity: O(n^2) time and output size per test (sum of n^2 <= 5e5)
dry_run: Final: a11 = 2 (C1), a12 = 2 (C2), a21 = 2 (R2), a22 = 1 (C2). Sum = 7, matching the sample total.
Formula check: k=1 gives T(0)+T(1) = 0+2; k=2 gives T(1)+T(2) = 2+3; total 7.

brief: A tree with n vertices loses all of its leaves at once in each operation (a single vertex or a two-vertex tree loses everything). After k operations, print how many vertices remain.
key_idea: Vertex v is removed in round r(v) = 1 + (second-largest branch length from v), so answer = number of v with r(v) > k; compute branch lengths with a rerooting DFS.
solution: Root the tree at 1 and get a BFS order with parents.
down[v] = longest downward path length; process vertices in reverse BFS order.
up[v] = longest path from v going through its parent; process in BFS order: for each vertex take the two largest branch lengths (children give down[c]+1, parent gives up[v]).
For child c of v, up[c] = 1 + (largest branch of v other than c's branch).
r(v) = (second-largest branch of v, or 0 if fewer than two branches) + 1. Answer = count of v with r(v) > k.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 4: n=5, k=1, path 3-2-1-5-4. Branch values: vertex 3 r=1, vertex 2 r=2 (branches 2 and 1 so second = 1, r = 2), vertex 1 r=3, vertex 5 r=2, vertex 4 r=1.
Count of r > 1: vertices 2, 1, 5 gives 3, matching the sample output 3.
Sample 2: n=2, k=200000, both vertices have r = 1, count 0, matching the sample.

brief: Given n integers summing to 0, rearrange them so that every contiguous subarray sum has absolute value strictly less than max(a) - min(a). Print No if impossible, otherwise Yes and one valid arrangement.
key_idea: Answer is No only when max = min (then all values are 0); otherwise greedily order by prefix sums: take a negative when the running sum is >= 0, else a positive, which keeps prefix sums in [min, max-1].
solution: If max == min, every element is 0 (sum is 0): print No.
Else max > 0 > min exists. Keep the prefix sum S starting at 0.
If S >= 0 and a negative remains, place a negative; if S >= 0 and none remain, the rest are zeros, place them; if S < 0, place a positive (one must exist since the total remaining is -S > 0).
Invariant: min <= S <= max-1 (positives are added only when S < 0, so S + y < max; negatives only when S >= 0, so S + x >= min).
All prefix sums including P_0 = 0 lie in [min, max-1], so any subarray sum P_j - P_i has |.| <= max-1-min < max-min.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 3 4 -2 -5, min -5, max 4 (need every |subarray sum| < 9). Greedy: S=0 take -2 (S=-2); S<0 take 3 (S=1); S>=0 take -5 (S=-4); S<0 take 4 (S=0). Output -2 3 -5 4, prefix sums 0,-2,1,-4,0 with range 5 < 9 (any valid answer is accepted).
Sample 2 check: prefix sums stay in [-5, 3], so the range is at most 8 < 9.
Sample 6: n=1, a = 0, max = min, print No.

brief: Books each have reading time t_i and flags a_i (Alice likes) and b_i (Bob likes). Choose a set containing at least k books Alice likes and at least k books Bob likes with minimum total time, or print -1 if impossible.
key_idea: Split books into 11, 10, 01 groups; for each count c of 11-books (cheapest c), take the cheapest max(0, k-c) books from each of 10 and 01 and minimize over c.
solution: Split books by (a,b): 11 (both like), 10 (Alice only), 01 (Bob only). Ignore 00 books.
Sort each group by time and build prefix sums.
For each c from 0 to |11|: need = max(0, k - c) books from 10 and from 01 each.
If need exceeds either group's size, skip c; otherwise candidate cost = P11[c] + P10[need] + P01[need].
Answer is the minimum candidate, or -1 if no c is feasible.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2: n=5, k=2. Groups: 11 = [2]; 10 = [5]; 01 = [1]; 00 books ignored.
c=0: need 2 from 10 but only 1 available, skip. c=1: need 1 each, cost 2 + 5 + 1 = 8.
Answer 8, matching the sample.
Sample 3: n=5, k=3. Groups: 11 empty, 10 = [2,3], 01 = [3,5]; c=0 needs 3 from each, skip; answer -1, matching the sample.

brief: Given a binary string s of even length n, build two balanced bracket sequences a and b of length n such that a_i = b_i where s_i = 1 and a_i != b_i where s_i = 0, or report NO.
key_idea: Write the ones as a shared +-1 walk X and the zeros as a shared-opposite walk Y; the best choice is X going up on the first half of ones and down on the second, and Y alternating 1,0,1,0 at zeros; feasible iff #1 and #0 are even and |Y| <= X at every prefix.
solution: Let T = count of 1s and Z = count of 0s. If T or Z is odd, answer NO (each balanced sequence has equal counts of '(' and ')', forcing even totals).
Track c = ones so far and k = zeros so far. At every prefix where k is odd, Y must be +-1, so we need 1 <= c <= T-1 (the ones-walk must be positive there); otherwise NO.
Construction: the j-th one gets '(' in both sequences if j < T/2, else ')' in both.
The k-th zero toggles Y between 1 (k odd) and 0 (k even); a gets '(' when Y rises, b gets '(' when Y falls.
Then bal_a = X + Y >= 0 and bal_b = X - Y >= 0 at every prefix, and both end at 0, so both are balanced.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 1: s = 101101, T = 4, Z = 2. Prefix checks: after zero 1 (c=1) ok, after zero 2 (k even) no check; output a = ((())), b = ()()() (valid, any answer accepted).
Sample 3: s = 1100, T = 2, Z = 2. The first zero comes at c = 2 = T with k = 1 odd, so c > T-1 fails: NO, matching the sample.
Own example: s = 10, T = 1 is odd, so the answer is NO immediately.

brief: Given array a and integer m, you may negate single elements. Find the minimum number of negations so that the prefix sum of the first m elements is no greater than every non-empty prefix sum.
key_idea: Split the work: the suffix of the first m elements (starting at index 2..m) must have sums <= 0, the piece after m must have prefix sums >= 0; fix each with a heap that negates the largest positive or most negative value on demand.
solution: Condition P_m <= P_j for j < m is equivalent to every sum a[j+1..m] <= 0 (j >= 1), i.e. every suffix starting at index 2..m is <= 0.
Condition P_m <= P_j for j > m is equivalent to every prefix sum of a[m+1..n] being >= 0.
Part 1: scan i from m down to 2, add a_i to a running sum and push it into a max-heap; while the sum > 0, pop the largest value v and negate it (sum decreases by 2v), count one op.
Part 2: scan i from m+1 to n, add a_i and push into a min-heap; while the sum < 0, pop the smallest v and negate it (sum increases by -2v), count one op.
The two parts use disjoint indices, so the answer is the total op count; a_1 is never useful to negate.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 2: a = 1 2 3 4, m = 3. Part 1, i=3: sum 3 > 0, pop 3, sum becomes -3, one op; i=2: sum -1, no op. Part 2: sum 4 >= 0, no op. Total 1, matching the sample.

Sample 5: a = -2 3 -5 -5 -20, m = 2. Part 1, i=2: sum 3 > 0, negate 3 (sum -3), one op. Part 2: i=3 sum -5 negate (sum 5); i=4 sum 0 fine; i=5 sum -20 negate -20 (sum 20). Total 3, matching the sample.

brief: Given a digit string a, you may swap two adjacent digits only if they have different parity. Output the smallest integer string reachable (leading zeros allowed) for each test case.
key_idea: Even digits keep their relative order among themselves and odd digits among themselves, and every interleaving is reachable, so merge the two subsequences by always taking the smaller front digit.
solution: Split the digits into two lists: evens (in original order) and odds (in original order).
Any merge of the two lists can be achieved by adjacent swaps of different parity, and no other reordering is possible.
Two-pointer merge: at each step output the smaller of the front even and front odd digit (if one list is empty, take from the other).
Output the merged string.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 0709, evens = [0,0], odds = [7,9]. Merge: 0 (0<7), 0 (0<7), then odds 7, 9: output 0079, matching the sample.
Sample 3: a = 246432, evens = [2,4,6,4,2], odds = [3]. Merge: 2 (2<3), 3 (4>3), then 4,6,4,2: output 234642, matching the sample.

brief: There are n heaps with h_i stones. In one pass over i = 3..n you choose d with 3d <= h_i, move d stones from heap i to i-1 and 2d to heap i-2. Maximize the size of the smallest heap after the pass.
key_idea: Binary search the target X; feasibility is checked by choosing d_i from the top index down, each as large as possible while heap i stays >= X (larger d_i only helps lower heaps), then checking heaps 1 and 2.
solution: Binary search X in [0, total stones]; X = 0 is always feasible.
Final heap j = h_j - 3*d_j + d_{j+1} + 2*d_{j+2} (d_k = 0 outside 3..n), and step i sees heap i still at h_i, so 3*d_i <= h_i.
For check(X): for i = n down to 3, need h_i + d_{i+1} + 2*d_{i+2} - X >= 0; set d_i = min(h_i/3, (h_i + d_{i+1} + 2*d_{i+2} - X)/3).
Finally need h_1 + 2*d_3 >= X and h_2 + d_3 + 2*d_4 >= X.
Answer is the largest X passing check; monotone because lower X is easier.
complexity: O(n log(sum h)) time, O(n) space per test case
dry_run: X = 8 fails at heap1 (1 + 2*3 = 7), so answer 7, matching the sample.

brief: Monocarp's rooted tree (root 1) was traversed by BFS where children are enqueued in ascending order; given the visiting order a, print the minimum possible height of such a tree.
key_idea: Cut the order into consecutive BFS levels; a level may be as long as possible as long as its number of increasing runs does not exceed the size of the previous level (each parent owns one ascending run of children).
solution: Each BFS level is a contiguous block of a. Children of one parent form one block segment that must be increasing (children are enqueued in ascending order).
So a block B_{k+1} needs at least (number of descents in B_{k+1}) + 1 runs, and each run belongs to a distinct parent in B_k; the condition is runs <= |B_k|.
Greedy: start with the root level [a_1]; from the start p of the next level, extend it while the run count stays <= size of the previous level.
Longer levels give more parents for the next level, so the greedy extension is optimal.
Count the levels built (after the root); this count is the minimum height.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space per test case
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 1 4 3 2. Level 0 = [1], size 1. Next level from 4: adding 3 creates a descent (2 runs > 1), so level 1 = [4]. Then [3] and [2] similarly: 3 levels, height 3, matching the sample.
Sample 3: a = 1 2 3. Level 1 starts at 2 with size 1; no descents, so the whole rest [2,3] is one level: height 1, matching the sample.

brief: Given a non-decreasing array a with a_i <= i, build an array b such that the MEX of the first i elements of b equals a_i for every i, or print -1.
key_idea: When the MEX must jump from prev to a_i, every value strictly between them must already be present; fill those 'gap' values at the earlier steps where a_i equals the current MEX (in increasing order), and at a jump place b_i = prev.
solution: Let prev = 0 (MEX of empty prefix). If a_i < prev, print -1 (cannot happen for non-decreasing input).
Collect all gap values G = the integers strictly between a_{i-1} and a_i for every jump i, in increasing order.
Scan i = 1..n. If a_i == prev (no change), set b_i to the next unused gap value from G, or to 10^6 if none remain; such values are above the MEX so MEX stays prev.
If a_i > prev (jump), check that every value in (prev, a_i) was already placed; if not, print -1. Otherwise set b_i = prev, which makes the MEX become a_i.
Update prev = a_i and continue; print b.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2: a = 0 0 0 2. G = [1] (gap between 0 and 2). i=1,2,3 equal to 0: b_1 = 1 (gap placed), b_2 = b_3 = 10^6. i=4 jump to 2: value 1 placed, b_4 = 0. Output 1 1000000 1000000 0.
Check: prefix MEX of [1] is 0, [1,10^6] is 0, [1,10^6,10^6] is 0, all 4 is 2. Valid, and the sample accepts any answer.
Sample 3: a = 1 1 3. i=1 jump: b_1 = 0. i=2 equal: G = [2], b_2 = 2. i=3 jump 1 -> 3: 2 placed, b_3 = 1. Output 0 2 1, matching the sample.

brief: n candidates each with a_i supporters, plus c undecided voters who vote for the lowest-numbered candidate still in the race. Excluding a candidate sends their supporters to the lowest remaining candidate. For each i, print the minimum number of other candidates to exclude so that candidate i wins (ties go to the lower number).
key_idea: Partially derived only: if the lowest kept candidate is i itself, exclude all earlier candidates and then greedily exclude the largest later candidates; a lower kept candidate L changes the cost and was not fully optimized, so no code is given.
solution: Let L be the lowest candidate kept. All candidates below L must be excluded, and all excluded votes go to L.

Case L = i: i's votes are c + (sum of a_j for j < i) + a_i + (sum of excluded later candidates). Every later candidate with a_j greater than the current votes must be excluded; process later candidates in decreasing a_j, excluding while a_j exceeds the running total.

Case L < i: i's votes are just a_i, and L's total c + a_1..a_L-prefix + forced exclusions must stay strictly below a_i. Choosing L well (trading the cost L-1 against forced exclusions) was not worked out here.
Full solution requires minimizing over L for each i efficiently; this record is incomplete.
Sample check: for sample 2 (c=3, a = 0 10) candidate 2 wins with 0 exclusions because candidate 1 has only c + a_1 = 3 < 10, which is case L < i and is essential.
complexity: not established
dry_run: Sample 2: n=2, c=3, a = 0 10. Candidate 2: lowest kept is 1 with votes 3 < 10, so answer 0, matching the sample.
Candidate 1 with case L = 1: votes 3, candidate 2 has 10 > 3 must be excluded, cost 1, matching the sample's first output.

brief: Build an n x n 0/1 grid with exactly k ones minimizing f = (max row sum - min row sum)^2 + (max column sum - min column sum)^2. Print the minimum f and one grid achieving it.
key_idea: The answer is 0 when n divides k and 2 otherwise; place ones along the cyclic diagonals (cell index t goes to row t mod n, column (t div n + t mod n) mod n) so both row and column sums differ by at most 1.
solution: If k % n == 0, all rows and all columns can have equal sums, so f = 0.
If k % n != 0, rows cannot all be equal and columns cannot all be equal (their sums add to k), so both spreads are >= 1 and f >= 2.
Fill the t-th one (t = 0..k-1) at row t % n and column (t / n + t % n) % n.
Each block of n consecutive t hits every column exactly once, so column sums differ by at most 1; rows also differ by at most 1.
Print f, then the n rows of the grid.
complexity: O(n^2) time and output per test case
dry_run: Sample n=2, k=2: 2 % 2 == 0 so f = 0, matching the sample.

brief: n cities on a line each have two portals of different colors among B, G, R, Y. Moving between two cities that share a color costs their distance. For each query (x, y), print the minimum travel cost from x to y, or -1 if impossible.
key_idea: If x and y share a color, the answer is |x-y|; otherwise go through one intermediate city z that shares a color with both, and for each compatible portal type only the nearest such city to x on each side matters.
solution: Let x <= y (the cost is symmetric). If x == y, answer 0.
If the two portal types share a color, answer y - x (no path can be cheaper than the distance).
Otherwise a route is x -> z -> y, cost |x-z| + |z-y|, where z's type shares a color with x's type and with y's type.

For each of the 6 types compatible with both, precompute the nearest city <= x (left) and >= x (right) of that type; cost is minimized by the nearest on each side, since for z between x and y the cost is constant and outside it grows with distance.
Answer = minimum candidate, or -1 if there is none. Precomputation is O(6n) per test.
complexity: O(6n + 6q) time, O(6n) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 1 (n=4): types BR BR GY GR. Query (3,1): swap to x=1 (BR), y=3 (GY), no shared color. Compatible type GR at city 4 is nearest right of x: cost (4-1) + |4-3| = 4, matching the expected 4.
Query (1,4): BR and GR share R, cost 3, matching.
Sample 2 query (1,2) with BG and RY: no shared color and no third city, so -1, matching.

brief: Two n x m matrices a and b each hold a permutation of 1..n*m. Swapping any two rows or any two columns is allowed. Decide whether a can be turned into b.
key_idea: Each value v gives a row pair (row in a -> row in b) and a column pair; a row (or column) permutation exists iff these pairs define consistent, one-to-one maps.
solution: Record for each value v its position (r_a, c_a) in a and (r_b, c_b) in b.
A row permutation sigma and column permutation tau must satisfy sigma(r_a) = r_b and tau(c_a) = c_b for every value v.
Keep rowTo[r_a] and rowFrom[r_b] arrays; any conflict (a row mapping to two different rows, or two rows mapping to one) gives NO. Do the same for columns.
If no conflict appears over all values, the maps are bijections on rows and columns, so the answer is YES.
Because both matrices contain every value exactly once, all rows and columns are covered.
complexity: O(n*m) time and space per test case
dry_run: Sample 3 (3x3 with values 1..9 in a and b): value 1 maps (0,0)->(0,0), value 2 maps (2,1)->(1,2)? a row 2 maps to b row 1 while another value of a row 2 would map to a different row, giving a conflict, so NO.
Sample 2 (2x2 with 1 2 / 3 4 and 4 3 / 2 1): rows 0->1, 1->0 and columns 0->1, 1->0 consistently, so YES.

brief: Build a one-row keyboard with all 26 lowercase letters so that every pair of adjacent characters in the password s is adjacent on the keyboard. Print NO if impossible, otherwise YES and one valid layout.
key_idea: Consecutive letters in s form edges of a graph; the layout exists iff this graph is a union of simple paths (every degree <= 2, no cycle), and listing each path in order gives a valid keyboard.
solution: Build an undirected graph on the 26 letters with an edge for every adjacent pair in s.
If any letter has degree > 2, print NO (a keyboard neighbor has only two sides).
Walk each path starting from a letter of degree <= 1, appending letters in order, marking them visited.
If some letter is still unvisited after all walks, it lies on a cycle: print NO.
Otherwise print YES and the concatenation of all walks (letters absent from s are singleton paths, so the result has all 26 letters).
complexity: O(26^2) time per test case
dry_run: Sample s = zxzytyz: edges z-x, z-y, y-t. Degrees: z=2, x=1, y=2, t=1. Walk from x: x z y t; then the rest a..w in order, output xzytabcdefghijklmnopqrsuvw, which is a valid layout.
Sample s = abcda: edges a-b, b-c, c-d, d-a form a cycle, so letters a, b, c, d stay unvisited: NO, matching the sample.

brief: Days 1..n each have a movie with value a_i. Kolya may watch at most m movies; each visit on day i after previous visit p costs d*(i-p) (previous visit starts at day 0). Maximize total value minus penalties; watching nothing gives 0.
key_idea: Penalties telescope to d times the last watched day, so total = sum of chosen a_i - d*last; fix the last day j and add the best (m-1) positive values before it, kept with a min-heap.
solution: For chosen days i1 < ... < ik, penalties are d*i1 + d*(i2-i1) + ... = d*ik, so the value is sum a - d*ik.
Fix the last chosen day j: the value is a_j - d*j + (best sum of up to m-1 chosen values from days 1..j-1).
Best up-to-(m-1) subset of a prefix = the largest m-1 positive values seen so far; maintain them with a min-heap and running sum S.
For j = 1..n: candidate = a_j - d*j + S; then insert a_j into the heap (if positive, replacing the smallest when full).
Answer = max(0, all candidates).
complexity: O(n log m) time, O(m) space per test case
dry_run: Sample 1: n=5, m=2, d=2, a = 3 2 5 4 6. Keep at most one earlier value. j=3: a_3 - 6 + S, where S = 3 (largest earlier value), gives 5 - 6 + 3 = 2.
Other j give 1, 1, -1, -1 at most, so the answer is 2, matching the sample.
Sample 2: n=4, m=3, d=1, a all 1: best candidate is 0 (watch nothing), matching the sample.

brief: n queues start at 0. Over n steps, every queue gains a_ij customers at step j, then Nikyr serves one queue (resetting it to 0). Choose the service order to maximize the MEX of the final queue lengths.
key_idea: Partially analyzed: a queue's final value is the sum of its additions after its last service, so each queue offers a decreasing set of values by service time; the matching of target values 0..m-1 to queues and service steps was not solved.
solution: Final x_i = sum of a_ij over steps j after queue i's last service (all steps if never served).
Value 0 needs a queue served at step n. Distinct queues need distinct last-service steps, and any set of distinct last-service steps can be completed to a valid schedule.
So MEX m requires, for each target value k in 0..m-1, a distinct (queue, step) pair with exactly that suffix sum; this is a rainbow-style matching that was not resolved here.
No code is provided because the matching step was not verified.
Answer is at most n.
complexity: not established
dry_run: Sample 1: n=2, a = [1 2; 2 1]. Serve queue 2 at step 1 then queue 1 at step 2: final x = [0, 1] (queue 2 after step 2 has 1), MEX 2, matching the sample.
Sample 2: n=2, a = [10 10; 10 10]. Serving queue 1 both times gives x = [0, 20], MEX 1, matching the sample.

brief: You hold a_i cards labeled i (n types), and may buy up to k more cards of any labels 1..n. Split all cards into decks of equal size with no repeated label inside a deck. Print the maximum deck size.
key_idea: Deck size d works iff some deck count M satisfies M >= max a_i and S <= M*d <= S+k (S = sum a_i); this is checked directly for each d from n down to 1.
solution: Let S = sum a_i, mx = max a_i. With M decks of size d, each label appears at most M times, so M >= mx is needed; after buying, the total must be exactly M*d.
Any total between S and S+k can be reached with up to k purchases as long as no label exceeds M (buy where counts are below M), so the condition is S <= M*d <= S+k with M >= mx.
For fixed d the valid M form the interval [max(mx, ceil(S/d)), floor((S+k)/d)]; d is feasible iff this interval is non-empty.
Deck size is at most n (distinct labels), so scan d from n down to 1 and output the first feasible d.
Checked by hand against all nine sample cases of this problem.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=3, k=1, a = 3 2 2, S = 7, mx = 3. d=3: interval [max(3,3), floor(8/3)=2] is empty. d=2: [max(3,4)=4, floor(8/2)=4] = {4}, feasible, answer 2.
Sample 4: n=10, k=8, S = 62, mx = 10. d=7: [max(10, 9), floor(70/7)=10] = {10}, feasible; d=8 gives [10, 8], empty. Answer 7, matching the sample.

brief: Each item costs 2 rubles, but after buying b_i items in total (of any kind), every further item of product i costs 1. Lena must end with at least a_i items of product i for each i. Find the minimum total cost.
key_idea: Assume exactly N = sum a_i items are bought; an item at position p (1-indexed) is discounted iff p > b_i, so maximize the number of discounted items with a sweep over positions where an item becomes eligible at b_i + 1 and each position takes one waiting eligible item.
solution: Buying extra items never helps, so buy exactly N = sum a_i items; cost = 2N - (number of discounted items).
Item of product i placed at position p is discounted iff at least b_i items were bought before it, i.e. p > b_i. A discounted slot needs an item already eligible.
Sort products by b_i. Sweep positions in increasing order with a pool of eligible items; product i's a_i items join the pool at position e_i = min(b_i + 1, N + 1).
Between events, each position consumes one pooled item if the pool is non-empty (counted as a discounted item); advance the position to each e_i in sorted order and add a_i to the pool.
After the last event, the remaining positions up to N consume the pool. Answer = 2N - matched.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: N = 5; products (a,b) = (1,3), (3,4), (1,5). Sweep: pos 1->4 with empty pool; add 1 (pool 1). Pos 4->5 consumes 1 (matched 1), add 3 (pool 3). Pos 5->6 consumes 1 (matched 2). Answer 2*5 - 2 = 8, matching the sample.
Sample 2: N = 8; sorted by b: (1,2), (2,4), (2,7), (1,8), (2,8). Matches 0 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 4; answer 16 - 4 = 12, matching the sample.
